teaser: The swing that launched a thousand chocolate boxes, and made its painter famous overnight.
review_notes:
Gift of Steven and Alexandra Cohen to the Met, 2012, after years on loan: check wording.
First owner John Wolfe, New York; shown at the Salon of 1873.
Reproductions on fans, porcelain and tapestries are mentioned by the Met; later uses (posters, puzzles, calendars) are stated generally.
Cot born 1837 in Bédarieux, pupil of Cabanel and close to Bouguereau, died 1883 aged 46.
Dimensions 213.4 x 127 cm.

lesson.text: You may never have heard the name Pierre-Auguste Cot, yet you have probably met this couple. They have swung on candy tins, jigsaw puzzles, dorm-room posters, greeting cards and embroidery kits for a century and a half. Few paintings have been reproduced so often by people who could not name the artist.

The copying started almost at once. Cot showed Springtime at the Paris Salon of 1873, the huge official exhibition of the year, and it was the crowd's favorite. Within a few years the image was printed as engravings and painted onto fans, porcelain and tapestries.

The picture left France quickly. A New York collector, John Wolfe, bought it and hung it in his Manhattan home, where it impressed visitors so much that his cousin ordered a second Cot of her own, The Storm.

Why did it travel so well? Partly because the story needs no caption. Two very young people share a swing in a green wood. He holds the ropes. She holds him. Everything else in the picture is there to say “first love” one more time.
Cot even hides a tiny pair in the leaves that repeats the big pair on the swing. Painters of his time loved this kind of echo: a small symbol that tells you how to read the main scene.
Another couple is flying through this forest. Where are they?

spots.title: Two butterflies
spots.text: Two pale yellow butterflies flutter side by side above the boy's head. In old paintings butterflies often stand for young love: light, short-lived, always in pairs.

lesson.text: The butterflies also set the clock. Butterflies, new leaves, wildflowers: this is April or May, and the title does double duty. Springtime names the season and the age of the two sitters, who look about fifteen.
Springtime shows love as a season: everything in the picture is new, light, and not built to last.

The finish is what made the picture a sensation. Cot trained in the academic system, the official art schooling of France, which prized smooth, invisible brushwork. Skin had to look like skin, with no trace of the hand that painted it. Wander around and see how far he took it.

spots.title: Her sideways look
spots.text: Her head rests on his arm, but her eyes slide up toward him with a teasing half-smile. She is the one in charge of this flirtation.

spots.title: His hidden face
spots.text: We see only dark curls and a cheek. Cot keeps the boy almost anonymous, so the girl's expression carries the whole scene.

spots.title: Grip on the rope
spots.text: His hand closes around a thick, hairy rope. The rough fibers are painted strand by strand, a contrast with the smooth skin next to them.

spots.title: The veil dress
spots.text: Her dress is closer to mist than cloth. Thin, transparent paint lets the warm tone of her legs show through, a showpiece of academic skill.

spots.title: The plank
spots.text: A plain block of wood is the seat. It is the only hard, square thing in a picture made of curves.

spots.title: Tangled feet
spots.text: Her foot hooks around his ankle. The two bodies are knotted together from arms to toes, so the pair reads as one swinging shape.

spots.title: Irises
spots.text: Purple irises rise from the reeds in the corner, next to a glimpse of water. Spring flowers, placed where a stage designer would put them.

lesson.text: That mix, rough rope against polished skin, is the whole academic recipe in one glance. It is also why modern critics turned against pictures like this. To eyes trained on Monet, who was painting his loose harbor sunrise around the same time, such perfection looked cold and sugary.
Cot did not enjoy his fame for long. He died in 1883 at the age of 46, only ten years after this triumph. His two swinging and running couples are almost all that the public remembers of him.

The canvas itself is big, more than 2 meters (about 7 feet) tall, and it stayed in private hands for well over a century. It finally joined the Metropolitan Museum's collection in 2012, in the same museum as the picture it inspired. The chocolate boxes had been famous far longer than the original.

quiz.question: Where was Springtime first shown to the public?
quiz.explanation: It was the crowd's favorite at the Salon of 1873.

quiz.question: Which small creatures echo the couple on the swing?
quiz.explanation: A pair of yellow butterflies flies above the boy's head.

quiz.question: What did the academic system prize in a painting's surface?
quiz.explanation: Skin had to look like skin, with no trace of the painter's hand.

quiz.question: What does the title refer to?
options: Only the month it was painted
The season and the youth of the couple
quiz.explanation: Springtime names both the time of year and the age of the sitters.

facts.text: Springtime was reproduced on fans, porcelain and tapestries soon after it was shown.
facts.explanation: Its Salon success led to copies on all kinds of objects.

facts.text: Cot lived to enjoy fifty years of fame after Springtime.
facts.explanation: He died in 1883 at 46, only ten years later.

facts.text: The boy's face is the most detailed part of the painting.
facts.explanation: His face is almost hidden; the girl's expression carries the scene.
